title: Discussing and Questioning New Words
keyIdea: When you meet a word you do not know, stop and ask: what does it mean? Look for clues in the picture and in the words around it. Test your guess by putting it in the gap: does the sentence still make sense? Then link the new word to a word you know, like enormous means really, really big. A word you know can also have a new meaning, so check the clues.

kid: Sometimes you read a word you do not know. Stop! Ask: what does this word mean?
Look for clues. The picture can help. The words next to it can help too. Sam was famished. He ate three bowls of soup! Soup is a clue. Famished means very hungry.

Test your guess. Put your word in the gap. Does the sentence still make sense? Then your guess is good. Join the new word to a word you know. Enormous is like big, only more. It means really, really big.
A word you know can mean a new thing. A bat can fly, or you can hit a ball with a bat. The other words tell you which one.
adult: This topic runs from about age 5 to 11. Children ask and answer questions about unknown words, use pictures and the words around a word (context) to work out a meaning, and explain the new word by linking it to one they know. It sits behind reading comprehension: a child who decodes a word but skips its meaning loses the sense of the sentence.

The habit to model is thinking aloud while you read together. Pause at a new word and say: "Hmm, what does gigantic mean? Let's look for clues." Point to the picture, reread the sentence, try your guess in the gap, then link it: "Gigantic is like big, but even bigger." Talking about words like this, rather than just giving a definition, is how most new words stick.

Common mistakes: skipping the word and reading on; guessing from what it looks or sounds like (famished is not famous, scalding is not scolding); choosing a meaning that does not fit the rest of the sentence; and assuming a familiar word keeps its usual meaning (a duck's bill is its beak). Be careful too: clues often give a rough meaning, not an exact one, so check tricky words in a children's dictionary together.

In the lab your child stops to ask about "enormous" and finds the picture clue, taps the clue words that show "famished" means very hungry, swaps guesses into a gap and watches the picture react, links four new words to words they know, and matches pictures to bat and bill in different sentences.

familyTip: At story time, choose one new word on each page. Ask "What do you think it means? What's your clue?" Try the guess in the sentence together, then link it to a word your child knows: "So enormous is like big, only bigger."

practice.prompt: Mia read: "The puppy was soaked after it jumped in the pond." What does soaked mean?
practice.hint: What happens to a puppy when it jumps in a pond?
practice.explain: The clue is jumped in the pond. A puppy that jumps in water gets very wet, so soaked means very wet.

practice.prompt: Leo found {n} gigantic pumpkins. Each one was too heavy to lift! What does gigantic mean?
practice.hint: Find the clue: what could Leo not do with each pumpkin?
practice.explain: Too heavy to lift is the clue. Gigantic means really big, like giant.

practice.prompt: You read a word you do not know. What should you ask?
choices: How many letters does it have?
practice.hint: Which question helps you understand the sentence?
practice.explain: Ask what the word means. Then look for clues in the picture and the words around it.

practice.prompt: Grandma said the cookies were scrumptious. Ben ate {n} of them and asked for more! What does scrumptious mean?
practice.hint: Why would Ben ask for more cookies?
practice.explain: Ben ate lots and asked for more, so the cookies must be very tasty. Scrumptious means very tasty.

practice.prompt: "I heard the phone ring." What does ring mean here?
choices: A thing you wear on a finger
practice.hint: The clue words are heard and phone.
practice.explain: You hear a phone ring, so here ring is a sound. The same word can also mean a ring for your finger.

pool.prompt: Tom was exhausted after the race. He lay down on the grass. What does exhausted mean?
pool.hint: What did Tom do after the race?
pool.explain: He lay down after a race, so exhausted means very tired.

pool.prompt: The sky was gloomy. Dark clouds hid the sun for {n} days. What does gloomy mean?
pool.hint: The clue is dark clouds hid the sun.
pool.explain: Dark clouds and no sun make a gloomy sky, so gloomy means dark and grey.

pool.prompt: Ava thinks famished means famous because the words look alike. What should she do?
pool.hint: Looking alike is not a clue. What else can help?
pool.explain: Words that look alike can mean very different things. Ava should look at the words around it to check.

pool.prompt: Dan gave his dog {n} treats. The dog was elated and wagged its tail. Which word you know is like elated?
pool.hint: How does a dog feel when it wags its tail?
pool.explain: A dog that gets treats and wags its tail is very happy. Elated is like happy, only more.

pool.prompt: What is a good way to check your guess for a new word?
choices: Put it in the gap and see if it makes sense
See if it starts with the same letter
pool.hint: Try your word in the sentence. What do you listen for?
pool.explain: Put your guess where the new word was. If the sentence still makes sense, your guess is good.

pool.prompt: "Fish swim in the stream." What is a stream?
pool.hint: Think about where fish live and swim.
pool.explain: Fish swim in water, so a stream must be water. A stream is a small river.

pool.prompt: "Please put the letter in the post box." What is the letter here?
choices: A sign like A or B
pool.hint: The clue words are post box.
pool.explain: You post a note, so here letter means a note you send. Letter can also mean A, B or C.

pool.prompt: Raj said, "The baby mouse is minute." Mum said, "Yes, tiny!" Which word you know is like minute here?
pool.hint: Mum gives a clue. What did she say?
pool.explain: Mum said tiny, so minute here means very small. Said this way, minute is a new word, not the minute on a clock.

pool.prompt: Kim put on her coat, hat and gloves. "It is chilly today," she said. What does chilly mean?
pool.hint: Why do people wear a coat, hat and gloves?
pool.explain: You wear a coat, hat and gloves when it is cold. Chilly means cold.

visual.caption: "Sam was famished. He ate three bowls of soup!" Which words are clues to what famished means? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: stop and ask, find picture and word clues, test guesses in the gap, link new words to known ones, and find new meanings for bat and bill.
